section: 4. executing fast: vectorised execution and late materialisation
text: Row at a time Classic engines, Postgres and SQLite included, execute a plan as a tree of operators that pass one row at a time : the aggregate asks the scan for the next row, the scan decodes one row from a page, hands it up, and the aggregate adds one number.
label: core

label: core

section: 4. executing fast: vectorised execution and late materialisation

section: 4. executing fast: vectorised execution and late materialisation
text: For 10 million rows it means 10 million rounds of function calls, type checks and branches per operator, and the CPU spends most of its time on that overhead rather than on the additions.
label: core

section: 4. executing fast: vectorised execution and late materialisation
text: A vector at a time Vectorised execution passes a batch of values, a vector , between operators: in DuckDB 2,048 values of one column per call ( DuckDB execution format ).
label: core

section: 4. executing fast: vectorised execution and late materialisation
text: The per-call overhead is paid once per 2,048 values, and the inner loop is a tight loop over an array of one type, which the compiler turns into SIMD instructions and the CPU's caches and branch predictor love.
label: core

section: 4. executing fast: vectorised execution and late materialisation

text: Defaults and limits worth knowing (26.9 source, 2026-10-04) Inserts are not fsynced by default ( fsync_after_insert = 0, confirmed in the embedded server too): an acknowledged insert can be lost if the machine loses power before the OS flushes it.
